paras: The killing of Mose Hart was the shooting of a Black man by officers and armed citizens in Corinth, Mississippi, on May 20, 1903, after he opened fire in the mayor's court during his trial for carrying concealed weapons. Hart wounded his wife, fled, and barricaded himself in a house, which the crowd set on fire; when he ran out he was shot many times and killed. A wire story about a "posse of citizens" ran nationally, and Black papers later listed the case among the year's lynchings under the name "Mrs. Hart."

Hart had been arrested for carrying concealed weapons and was tried before Mayor Young in the mayor's office in Corinth. The local Corinthian described him as "a desperate negro" who was often in court and claimed that he had shot an officer at Lexington, Tennessee, before coming to Corinth. His wife was a witness against him.

According to the Corinthian's same-day report, the mayor had just sentenced Hart to jail at about 2:30 p.m. and, seeing him reach for a pistol, called on Officer Meeks to shoot; Hart fired first. As Black witnesses stampeded for the door, one shot passed close to Chief Bell, who fired back and hit the handle of Hart's pistol. Hart's wife was shot, and the officers' return fire missed him as he ran.

Pursued by Officer Meeks and Burt McCord, he ran toward the National Cemetery and entered George Nagle's house on the cemetery road, barricading the door as Mrs. Nagle and her child fled. A large crowd, many armed with Winchester rifles, surrounded the house and exchanged shots with him.

The crowd set the house on fire; the Washington Times and the Grenada Sentinel said the adjoining house burned too. Officers called on him to surrender, but he ran out and, within a few yards, was brought down by several shots and a load of buckshot from Meeks's gun. By the Corinthian's count, hardly an hour passed from first shot to death.
No report of an inquest, arrests or grand jury action, or of whether Hart's wife survived, appears in the coverage.

The Corinthian printed the shooting the same afternoon as "Wretch Riddled with Bullets" and followed with "The Tragic Matinee. Yesterday's Open Air Performance." It wrote that the harm Hart might have done with the Winchesters said to be at his home was "horrible to contemplate." The Grenada Sentinel, also in Mississippi, headed its account "Negro Fought to the Last" and called burning the two houses "necessary."

Elsewhere, a Corinth dispatch of May 21 said Hart had been shot "after an exciting battle" by "a posse of citizens" after using "insulting epithets" and firing on Marshal Bell. It ran on May 22 from Maine to Arizona under headlines such as "Negro Desperado Soon Taken Care of," "Invited Death," "Mississippi Citizens Put a Negro Out of the Way" and "Negro Killed by Mob." The Washington Times ran a fuller version as "Smoked Out and Killed by a Mob." Weekly digests cut it to a line, some saying he was "shot to death by a mob."

No Black newspaper account of the killing was found; the case reached the Black press only through lynching lists. The Wichita Searchlight listed "Mrs. Hart, colored, murderous assault, Corinth, Miss.," and the Seattle Republican printed the entry in a list headed "Mobocracy's Bloody Reign." A white tally from the Providence Journal used the same "Mrs. Hart" entry, though no report said Hart's wife was killed.

The Corinthian and the Washington Times said the mayor had just sentenced Hart and called on an officer to shoot; the posse wire said Hart fired when Bell was told to keep order; the Grenada Sentinel said he was awaiting an appeal bond. His wife was either shot in the back and expected to die, or shot accidentally and not seriously while trying to stop him.

The house appears as "a negro house," the Nagles' house, "a hut," "a vacant house" or "a white man's house." Wires said "last night" or "yesterday" and the Black lists gave the 21st, but the Corinthian, printed while Hart was still besieged, put the shooting on Wednesday afternoon.

reader.title: Killing of Mose Hart
bases: Hart was killed by officers (Meeks, McCord, Bell) and a large armed crowd that pursued him after he fired in the mayor's court, besieged and burned the house he hid in, and shot him as he ran out (A13, A14, A2); wires called the killers both a 'posse of citizens' and a 'mob' (A3, A2).

A crowd of many armed citizens, joined by officers, burned two houses and riddled Hart with bullets after he ran out, and wires and digests called it a killing 'by a mob' (A2, A13, A17); but Hart was armed and firing, officers led the pursuit and called on him to surrender (A14, A25), so whether the killing was outside the law is unclear, though a 1903 lynching tally and two Black-press lists counted the Corinth case (A30, A31, A32).

The local Corinthian (A13, A14), two separate wire versions (A2, A3), the Butler Weekly Times variant (A18) and the Grenada Sentinel (A25) agree that Hart fired in the mayor's court, fled, was besieged in a house that was burned, and was shot dead.

accounts.label: Local paper (Corinthian daily, same afternoon and next day)
accounts.gist: Mayor Young had sentenced Hart to jail and, seeing him reach for a pistol, called on Officer Meeks to shoot; Hart opened fire, shot his wife, fled, barricaded himself in George Nagle's house; the crowd burned it and shot him down as he ran out, buckshot from Meeks finishing him.

accounts.label: Washington Times wire
accounts.gist: Close to the local first report: sentence, mayor's call to shoot, wife shot at the street door and expected to die, two houses burned, Hart 'smoked out' and riddled; headed 'killed by a mob'.

accounts.label: Posse-of-citizens wire
accounts.gist: Hart used 'insulting epithets' before the mayor, fired on Marshal Bell when Bell was told to keep order, escaped to a hut near the cemetery, and was riddled when the house was fired; killed 'by a posse of citizens' 'after an exciting battle'.

accounts.label: Butler Weekly Times variant
accounts.gist: Convicted, Hart broke away and fired; his wife stepped in front of him and was shot in the back; he fled to a white man's house, then dashed for his own home and fell with over a score of bullets in him.

accounts.label: Grenada Sentinel (Mississippi)
accounts.gist: Convicted and waiting to make an appeal bond, Hart became unruly; his wife held his hand and was accidentally, not seriously, shot; burning two houses was 'necessary' and he 'came shooting'.

accounts.label: Black-press lynching lists
accounts.gist: Listed the Corinth case as a lynching on the 21st under the name 'Mrs. Hart, colored', one with the charge 'murderous assault'.

framing.detail: The local Corinthian headed its reports 'Wretch Riddled with Bullets' and 'The Tragic Matinee. Yesterday's Open Air Performance', praised the pursuers' daring, and dwelt on the harm Hart might have done.
The Grenada Sentinel's 'Negro Fought to the Last' said burning the houses was 'necessary'.
The posse wire ran from Maine to Arizona under headlines such as 'Negro Desperado Soon Taken Care of', 'Invited Death', 'Mississippi Citizens Put a Negro Out of the Way' and 'Negro Killed by Mob'.
Weekly digests compressed it to one line, some saying he was killed 'by a mob', one 'because of insulting language'.
The Seattle Republican placed the 'Mrs. Hart' entry in a 1903 list headed 'Mobocracy's Bloody Reign', likening the country to Russia and Turkey.
The Wichita Searchlight's list gave the entry as 'Mrs. Hart, colored, murderous assault, Corinth, Miss.'
